notes: Five quick guides for urgent moments. Short, scannable how-tos, not lessons: no quizzes, no practice, no Ollie (brand rule: no Ollie on crisis screens).
Placeholders as in quiz.json, singular labels as in lessons ({recipient}, {Recipient}, {possessive}, {object}).
Layout per guide: title → 'Call 911 now if' box (red, always first when present) → numbered steps → 'Then' → 'Don't' → resources with tap-to-call → footer line.
Highlight rules ('For now') stay in plan-rules.json → quickGuides.
Every guide is reachable from the Plan tab and from the 'Need help now?' sheet, without a subscription check.
Phone numbers and the 15-minute missing-person rule come from the sources listed per guide. Re-check numbers before launch, and have a dementia-care or nursing professional review all five guides.
Nothing here diagnoses or treats. Medical decisions are routed to 911, the doctor or the pharmacist.
The 'After a hospital stay' steps are practical discharge questions, not clinical advice; have them reviewed with the other guides.

guides.title: If {recipient} goes missing
guides.summary: Search for up to 15 minutes, then call 911.
callNow: You've searched for 15 minutes and haven't found {object}
{Recipient} may be in danger right now: near traffic or water, in bad weather, or without needed medicine

steps.title: Start looking right away
steps.text: Don't wait to see if {recipient} comes back. Check the home first: closets, the garage, the yard, the car.

steps.title: Search nearby, in the likely direction
steps.text: Many people who wander are found within about 1.5 miles of where they were last seen. Look along the way to places {recipient} talks about: an old home, a former job, a church, a favorite store.

steps.title: After 15 minutes, call 911
steps.text: Say: "A person with dementia is missing. {Recipient} is a vulnerable adult." Police usually don't need to wait 24 hours in this case.

steps.title: Have the details ready
steps.text: A recent photo, height, weight, what {recipient} was wearing, where {recipient} was last seen, and any medicines {recipient} needs.

steps.title: Ask for help
steps.text: Call neighbors and family. If you need help being taken seriously, the Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline can talk with responders.

then: When {recipient} is found, stay calm and warm. Don't scold; {recipient} may be frightened.
If {recipient} was out in heat or cold, or seems hurt or more confused than usual, get medical help.
Afterwards, make a plan: a recent photo on your phone, a list of likely places, ID jewelry or a wandering response service, and a note to neighbors.
dont: Don't wait more than 15 minutes to call 911.
Don't search alone for long: call others in.

sources.name: Alzheimer's Association, wandering and emergency preparedness

guides.title: After a fall
guides.summary: Check before you lift. When in doubt, call 911.
callNow: {Recipient} hit {possessive} head, or you're not sure
{Recipient} passed out, even briefly, or is more confused or drowsy than usual
There's severe pain, or pain in the hip, back or neck
{Recipient} can't move an arm or leg, or a limb looks out of shape
{Recipient} can't get up, even with your help

steps.title: Don't lift right away
steps.text: Get down to {possessive} level. Say calmly: "I'm here. Let's not move yet."

steps.title: Check before moving
steps.text: Ask where it hurts. Look for bleeding, swelling or a limb at an odd angle. Ask if {recipient} hit {possessive} head.

steps.title: If anything on the 911 list is true
steps.text: Call 911. Don't move {object}. Keep {object} warm with a blanket and stay close until help arrives.

steps.title: If {recipient} is not hurt and wants to get up
steps.text: Bring a sturdy chair close. Let {object} roll to one side, get onto hands and knees, and use the chair to rise slowly while you steady {object}. Stop if anything hurts.

steps.title: If you can't help safely
steps.text: Don't lift {object} on your own. Make {object} comfortable on the floor and call for help.

then: Tell {possessive} doctor about the fall the same day, even if {recipient} seems fine. Mention it if {recipient} takes blood thinners.
Watch for the next 24 hours: new headache, vomiting, more sleepiness or confusion than usual means call 911.
Write down when and where it happened; add it to the doctor-visit sheet.
Look at what caused it: a rug, poor light, a step, getting up at night.
dont: Don't pull {object} up by the arms.
Don't give food or drink while you wait for an ambulance.

sources.name: UCLA Health, falls in older adults (cites National Institute on Aging)

guides.title: A sudden change in confusion
guides.summary: Sudden confusion is not 'just the dementia'. Get help today.
callNow: Signs of a stroke: one side of the face droops, one arm is weak, speech is slurred or strange
{Recipient} is hard to wake, or passes out
Fever with shivering, cold or clammy skin, a fast pulse, or very fast or slow breathing
The confusion started after a head injury
{Recipient} has diabetes and the confusion came on suddenly

steps.title: Notice how fast it changed
steps.text: Dementia changes slowly, over months. A big change over hours or a day or two is different, and often has a cause that can be treated.

steps.title: Keep {object} safe and calm
steps.text: Stay with {object}, speak softly, keep the room quiet and lit. Don't argue with what {recipient} says.

steps.title: If nothing on the 911 list is true, call the doctor today
steps.text: Call {possessive} doctor's office or after-hours line now, not tomorrow. A nurse can tell you whether to come in, go to urgent care or go to the emergency room.

steps.title: Tell them what changed
steps.text: When it started, what's different from {possessive} usual, and anything new: a new medicine, a fall, a fever, drinking less, trouble passing urine, pain, poor sleep.

steps.title: Bring the list
steps.text: If {recipient} goes to be seen, bring all {possessive} medicines (or photos of the labels) and your notes.

then: Confusion like this can come and go during the day. Better moments don't mean it's over: follow up until the cause is found.
Add what happened to the doctor-visit sheet.
dont: Don't wait until morning to see if it passes.
Don't give extra or new medicines to calm {object} unless a doctor or pharmacist tells you to.

sources.name: NHS, confusion: common causes in older people

guides.title: After a hospital stay
guides.summary: Ask the right questions before leaving, and make the first days calm.
callNow: New trouble breathing, chest pain, or signs of a stroke
{Recipient} is suddenly much more confused, very hard to wake, or can't keep fluids down

steps.title: Before leaving the hospital, ask
steps.text: What happened and what to watch for. Which medicines are new, changed or stopped. When the follow-up visit is and with whom. Whether home health care or equipment was ordered. Who to call with questions, day and night.

steps.title: Get it in writing
steps.text: Ask for the discharge papers and the updated medicine list. Take a photo of each page.

steps.title: Go over the medicines with the pharmacist
steps.text: Compare the new list with what's at home, so nothing old is taken by mistake.

steps.title: Make the first days calm
steps.text: Familiar room, a night light, a simple routine, water within reach, and the same short answers to the same questions.

steps.title: Expect more confusion for a while
steps.text: Many people with dementia are more confused after a hospital stay. Tell the doctor if it's getting worse instead of better, or if anything new appears.

then: Book the follow-up visit before you leave, or the next working day.
Ask family to cover the first few days; put tasks on the family board.
Do a quick safety check at home: clear paths, grab bars, lighting on the way to the bathroom.
dont: Don't leave without a written medicine list and a number to call.
Don't change doses on your own; ask the doctor or pharmacist.

guides.title: You're at your limit
guides.summary: You matter too. Here's what to do right now.
callNow: You're thinking about hurting yourself: call or text 988 now
You're afraid you might hurt {recipient}, or someone is in danger: call 911

steps.title: Make sure everyone is safe
steps.text: If {recipient} is safe for a few minutes, step into another room. It's okay to leave a hard moment and come back.

steps.title: Take one slow breath, then another
steps.text: Breathe out longer than you breathe in. Put your feet on the floor. Drink some water.

steps.title: Talk to someone now
steps.text: Call a person you trust, or the Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline. You can talk to them about how you feel, not just about {recipient}.

steps.title: Hand off one thing
steps.text: Ask a sibling, friend or neighbor to take one task today: a call, a visit, a meal.

steps.title: Plan a real break
steps.text: Respite care can give you hours or days off. The Eldercare Locator finds local respite and caregiver support.

then: Feeling angry, exhausted or resentful doesn't make you a bad daughter or son. It means you've been carrying too much alone.
When you have a few minutes, open the lesson 'Spotting burnout early' or 'A plan for your own breaks'.
If this happens often, tell your own doctor how you're doing.
dont: Don't wait until you're completely empty to ask for help.
Don't handle a dangerous moment alone: call.

sources.name: Administration for Community Living, Eldercare Locator
